newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Traders up 1997 China corn export estimates.
newsitem.headline: Traders up 1997 China corn export estimates.

text.p: Hong Kong and China traders said they would not be surprised if China exported up to four million tonnes of corn in 1997, noting that only a sharp drop in world corn prices would make Chinese corn uncompetitive.
"There is no limit to exports, if the price is right," said a senior Chinese trader.

China had already booked about 1.2 million tonnes of corn exports since the beginning of this year, another Chinese trader in Beijing estimated, and said that further tonnages would simply depend on whether world prices were favourable to Chinese exporters.
"I would agree with the higher estimates, it looks as though a lot of people have access to Chinese corn," a Singapore trader said.
A 20,000-tonne parcel of corn was heard sold to both Malaysia and Indonesia recently at about $133 per tonne, FOB China, but this could not be confirmed.
One trader said he heard another parcel of corn traded on Wednesday at $134 per tonne, FOB China, but no further details were available.
The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) corn price drop had not yet affected Chinese exports, grain sources said.
Corn closed on Wednesday with March down 3-1/2 at $3.08-1/2. Buyers were bearish on corn, some grain dealers said.

"I'm trying to sell, but all buyers are bearish corn to begin with and the strength of corn recently is due to the strength of beans, so once beans break, corn is going to tumble," a senior Hong Kong-based grains trader said.
Buyers were waiting for corn prices to drop below $150 per tonne, C&F Southeast Asia, he said.
Chicago soymeal also ended down with May off $7.80 at $266.00 per tonne, but the levels were still too high to attract Chinese buying, traders in Hong Kong and Singapore said.

"You get more inquiries, it's a bit closer to people's buying ideas, but it's still around $10-15 away," said one grains trader, noting that the market had earlier moved up too quickly to make the recent drop significant.
One trader estimated that if the market did drop another $10 dollars, China could well step in to buy a "couple of thousand tonnes" of soymeal.
"It tells you the market thinks the beans can break more," another source said.
